talat-noi.description: Talat Noi is an old Chinese-Thai neighbourhood near Bangkok’s Chao Phraya River. Around Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung 22, find murals, shrines, old homes and a museum in a former workshop.
intro: Talat Noi grew as trade in Sampheng expanded, forming a Chinese-Thai community of narrow lanes. Around Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung 22, you can see old houses and shrines, murals of daily life and festivals, and the distinctive orange Fiat.

Near the river, former workshops have also been converted into a museum and cafés. Look beyond the murals to the homes, workshops and riverside shrine to see traces of work and daily life in the neighbourhood. Residents still live here, so stick to public lanes and spaces.

experiences.title: A Chinese-Thai community and its workshops
paragraphs: Talat Noi developed as commerce in Sampheng grew, and remains a Chinese-Thai community. Old homes, shops and shrines stand close together along Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung 22.

The local museum tells the story of lathe workshops that made parts for boats, machinery and rice mills. Alongside the houses in the lanes, it gives a more concrete sense of the work and life in this riverside commercial district.

experiences.title: Festival murals and the orange Fiat
paragraphs: Murals in the lanes depict lion dances, festivals and residents’ lives. The orange Fiat in front of an old brick wall is another familiar neighbourhood scene.
The Fiat and murals are popular photo subjects, but nearby are people’s homes and workplaces. Leave doorways clear and make room for others to pass through the narrow lanes when taking pictures.

experiences.title: Riverside shrines and buildings put to new use
paragraphs: You can see the Hokkien-associated Chao Sue Kong Shrine, established in 1804, and Rong Kua Kue Shrine, connected with the Chinese merchant community. Trees and a small garden at the riverside pier offer a different view from the lanes.

Some old courtyard houses and parts of former workshops are now cafés or a local museum. Visit spaces that are open to the public, and respect private rooms and restricted areas as residents’ and operators’ spaces.

accessSections.title: Walk from Hua Lamphong station
paragraphs: The Tourism Authority of Thailand describes Talat Noi as about a 15-minute walk from Hua Lamphong station on the MRT Blue Line. Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung 22 are the featured lanes; the map pin marks the neighbourhood as a whole.

faq: Is Talat Noi a market where I can shop?

Although its name means “small market”, a visit is more about walking through the old Chinese-Thai neighbourhood around Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung 22 than visiting one market building. Look for lane murals, old houses, shrines, cafés and the workshop museum.
Which historic places can I visit?

The featured places include Chao Sue Kong Shrine, established in 1804, and Rong Kua Kue Shrine, connected with the Chinese merchant community. A local museum also tells the story of workshops that made parts for boats, machinery and rice mills.
Can I get there by train?

The Tourism Authority of Thailand describes a walk of about 15 minutes from Hua Lamphong station on the MRT Blue Line. Talat Noi covers lanes around Wanit 2 and Charoen Krung 22, so navigate to the lane or open-to-visitors place you want rather than looking for one entrance.

charoen-krung.title: Charoen Krung Bangkok: Historic Architecture, TCDC and Warehouse 30 | ThaiLiveNow
charoen-krung.description: Charoen Krung is a long riverside road in Bangkok with historic commercial buildings and design spaces. Visit TCDC in the Central Post Office and Warehouse 30 in converted warehouses on Charoen Krung 30.
intro: Charoen Krung is a long road and surrounding neighbourhood where historic commercial buildings and newer creative spaces line Bangkok’s riverside. Highlights include the Thailand Creative & Design Center (TCDC) inside the Central Post Office and Warehouse 30, a group of seven former warehouses on Charoen Krung 30.

After seeing the Central Post Office exterior, browse the bookshops, record shop and cafés beneath the old warehouse roofs. The two buildings have different uses. Charoen Krung is not one single attraction, so decide which places you want to visit first.

experiences.title: A design centre inside the Central Post Office
paragraphs: The old riverside commercial district’s Central Post Office building houses the Thailand Creative & Design Center (TCDC). See the grand exterior, then continue inside to the design-related spaces.
Seeing the building’s exterior and using TCDC’s exhibitions and facilities are different visits. What you can see inside depends on which spaces are open on the day.

experiences.title: Warehouse 30 in seven wartime warehouses
paragraphs: Warehouse 30 on Charoen Krung 30 is an arts destination reusing seven warehouses from the Second World War period. Shops selling clothing, homewares, books, flowers and records occupy the old structures.

Where the Central Post Office is a large public building housing a design centre, Warehouse 30 turns several low-rise logistics buildings into small shops and creative spaces. Visiting both shows how historic commercial buildings on Charoen Krung have found different new uses.

experiences.title: Food and event spaces inside the warehouses
paragraphs: Some warehouses contain cafés, restaurants and bars, so you can stop for a meal while browsing the shops. Places to eat and places to shop sit together inside the old buildings, with each warehouse used differently.

Warehouse Seven is a multipurpose venue for films, workshops and other events. Unlike a regular shop visit, individual events take place on specific dates, so what you find inside can vary with your visit day.

accessSections.title: Set your destination to the building you plan to visit
paragraphs: Charoen Krung is a long road. The Central Post Office (Grand Postal Building) and Warehouse 30 are separate buildings. The address 52–60 Soi Charoen Krung 30, Bang Rak is for Warehouse 30 alone.

faq: Is Charoen Krung one building or a fixed walking route?
No. Charoen Krung is a long road and surrounding neighbourhood. Choose the buildings you want to visit, such as the Central Post Office and TCDC or Warehouse 30 on Charoen Krung 30.
What can I see at Warehouse 30?

It reuses seven warehouses from the Second World War period. There are shops for clothing, homewares, books, flowers and records, along with cafés and restaurants; Warehouse Seven hosts films, workshops and other events.
Is the Warehouse 30 address an entrance to all of Charoen Krung?
No. 52–60 Soi Charoen Krung 30, Bang Rak is the address for Warehouse 30. If you want to visit the Central Post Office or another building, set that place as a separate destination.

nimmanhaemin.type: Chiang Mai neighbourhood of cafes, boutiques and galleries
nimmanhaemin.title: Nimmanhaemin Chiang Mai: Cafes, Boutiques and Gallery Lanes | ThaiLiveNow
nimmanhaemin.description: Nimmanhaemin is a Chiang Mai neighbourhood of cafés, galleries and boutiques along a roughly 1 km main road and its sois. Soi 1’s handmade goods, Soi 17’s gallery café and One Nimman are separate places.
intro: Nimmanhaemin is a Chiang Mai neighbourhood of cafés, galleries and boutiques along a roughly 1 km main road and its side sois. Small shops sit among homes, giving the main road and the lanes different characters.

On Soi 1, browse scented candles, natural-fibre paper and embroidered bags from the Sanjiang people. Soi 17 is home to artist Torlarp Larpcharoensook’s gallery café SS1254372. For shopping and dining in one complex, you can also visit One Nimman, a separate commercial development.
facts: Main road about 1 km · surrounding sois included

experiences.title: A neighbourhood of sois branching off the main road
paragraphs: Several sois branch off Nimmanhaemin’s roughly 1 km main road. Cafés, galleries and boutiques sit among residential streets, so stepping off the main road brings you to smaller-scale shops.
Soi 1 is known for shops selling scented candles, natural-fibre paper and Sanjiang embroidered bags. Browse the main-road stores and the smaller shops tucked between homes in the sois.

experiences.title: Lanes where galleries and cafés sit side by side
paragraphs: Cafés, galleries and home-goods shops sit among the houses in different sois. You might look at art, choose a gift and then stop at a café in another lane.
There are no shared opening hours for the whole neighbourhood. Check the opening days and hours of a particular gallery or restaurant before setting out.

experiences.title: Explore the gallery café and One Nimman
paragraphs: Soi 17 is home to artist Torlarp Larpcharoensook’s gallery café SS1254372. It brings together art, local coffee and tea, and meals made with seasonal produce.

One Nimman gathers shops selling regional Thai products, creative spaces, restaurants and cafés in one place. It is a different kind of commercial destination from the small shops in the sois; pop-ups and art events are available on the dates they take place.

accessSections.title: Getting to Nimmanhaemin in Chiang Mai
paragraphs: Nimmanhaemin’s main road and sois span the Suthep area of Chiang Mai. The Tourism Authority of Thailand describes it as about 15 minutes from the city centre by vehicle or songthaew. The location varies depending on whether you are heading to a handicraft shop on Soi 1 or the gallery café on Soi 17.

faq: Are Nimmanhaemin and One Nimman the same place?
One Nimman is a separate commercial complex within the Nimmanhaemin neighbourhood. Nimmanhaemin itself is a roughly 1 km main road and a network of sois with cafés, galleries and boutiques.
What can I see in the sois?
Soi 1 has shops selling scented candles, natural-fibre paper and Sanjiang embroidered bags. Soi 17 is home to artist Torlarp Larpcharoensook’s gallery café SS1254372.
Do all the shops in the neighbourhood share opening hours?
No. Cafés, galleries and boutiques each have their own hours, and One Nimman’s hours do not apply to the whole neighbourhood.

phuket-old-town.name: Phuket Old Town

phuket-old-town.type: Phuket historic district with shophouses and street art
phuket-old-town.title: Phuket Old Town: Sino-Portuguese Shophouses, Street Art and Local Food | ThaiLiveNow
phuket-old-town.description: Phuket Old Town preserves Sino-Portuguese shophouses from the tin-mining era, murals and the Thai Hua Museum. Local foods such as Hokkien noodles, dim sum and apong can also be found around the streets.
intro: Phuket Old Town has shophouses and mansions from the era when tin mining brought prosperity to the island. Sino-Portuguese buildings and murals preserve traces of the Peranakan community, where Chinese, Malay and Thai cultures met; some old buildings are now used as museums or cafés.

At Thai Hua Museum on Krabi Road, learn about the history of Phuket’s Chinese community, then try local foods such as Hokkien fried noodles, dim sum and apong. The Lard Yai market on Thalang Road is a Sunday event; the Old Town’s streets and buildings can be seen on other days too.

experiences.title: Shophouses from the tin-mining era
paragraphs: Shophouses and mansions built when Phuket prospered through tin mining remain in the Old Town. Their façades show the history of the island, where Chinese migrants and Malay and Thai cultures met, in buildings combining commercial and residential uses.

The Sino-Portuguese buildings along both sides of the road show an urban commercial side of Phuket, different from its beach resorts. Some historic buildings are still used as restaurants, cafés and accommodation, bringing the street’s past and present together.

experiences.title: Thai Hua Museum and street murals
paragraphs: Thai Hua Museum on Krabi Road is a place to explore the history and heritage of Phuket’s Chinese community. The museum building itself is also one of the Old Town’s historic buildings.

After visiting Thai Hua Museum, return to the street to see shophouses, murals and businesses that are still open. Seeing the museum and the commercial street together shows how Old Town’s architecture extends beyond a single exhibition room.

experiences.title: From Hokkien noodles to o-aew
paragraphs: Phuket’s local foods include Hokkien fried noodles, o-tao, loba and o-aew. Some places serve dim sum and dumplings or khanom chin rice noodles with curry in the morning; apong is a snack you can try as well.

Tasting local dishes at restaurants in the old streets is one way to experience the food culture left by Phuket’s different communities. Lard Yai Market on Thalang Road is held on Sundays and is a separate event from the Old Town itself.

faq: Can I visit Phuket Old Town only on Sundays?

No. The historic shophouses, murals and restaurants are part of the neighbourhood and can be visited on other days. Lard Yai Sunday Market is a separate event on Thalang Road, listed from 16:00 to 22:00 on Sundays.
Where can I learn more about the historic buildings?
Thai Hua Museum on Krabi Road covers the history and heritage of Phuket’s Chinese community. Sino-Portuguese shophouses from the tin-mining era and old mansions also remain along the streets.
What local foods can I try in the Old Town?
Local foods include Hokkien fried noodles, o-tao, loba and o-aew. In the morning, you can find dim sum, dumplings and khanom chin rice noodles with curry; apong is also available as a snack.

bophut-fishermans-village.name: Bophut Fisherman’s Village
bophut-fishermans-village.thai: หมู่บ้านชาวประมงบ่อผุด
bophut-fishermans-village.type: Historic fishing-village shopping street in Bophut
bophut-fishermans-village.title: Bophut Fisherman’s Village: Historic Shops, Crafts and Seaside Dining | ThaiLiveNow
bophut-fishermans-village.description: Fisherman’s Village Bophut is a street of former fishing-village homes, shops and restaurants along Koh Samui’s northern coast road. Browse crafts in old Chinese-style wooden shophouses and dine by the sea.
intro: Fisherman’s Village Bophut is a street of former fishing-village homes, shops and restaurants along Bophut Beach on Koh Samui’s north coast. Some old wooden shophouses belonging to the Chinese community have become shops and accommodation, so you can see both the buildings’ earlier character and today’s beachside businesses.

Along the coast road, browse small goods such as hand-carved soap, wooden ornaments and ceramics, then have seafood at a restaurant near the water. It suits a visit focused on old houses, shops and a meal more than a day of swimming at the beach.

experiences.title: A coast road where fishing-village homes became shops
paragraphs: Bophut is a northern Koh Samui beach area with a long fishing-village history. One feature of the street is the conversion of Chinese residents’ old shophouses into shops, accommodation and restaurants.

Along the coast road, you can see the wooden exteriors of old houses alongside the businesses that occupy them today. This is more of a street stroll with shop browsing and a restaurant stop than a day spent relaxing on the beach.

experiences.title: Hand-carved soap and local crafts
paragraphs: Souvenir shops sell hand-carved soap, wooden ornaments, ceramics, bags, jewellery and clothing. As you browse the small shops along the coast road, you can also look at the wooden buildings they occupy.

These shops are not gathered in one newly built beachfront mall. They occupy buildings along the old fishing-village road, where the wooden shophouses once used by Chinese residents stand beside their current shop interiors.

experiences.title: Dinner with a view of the sea
paragraphs: Restaurants along the coast road serve seafood and a range of international dishes. After browsing the souvenir shops, sit down at a restaurant near the water to enjoy Bophut’s beach and businesses in one evening.

As you walk along the coast road, shops on the old commercial side and restaurants facing the sea create different scenes. Seafood venues sit alongside restaurants serving international food, giving you an evening out that differs from simply relaxing on Bophut Beach.

accessSections.title: Distinguish Bophut Beach from Fisherman’s Village
paragraphs: Fisherman’s Village Bophut is the coast road along Bophut Beach on Koh Samui’s north coast, lined with former fishing-village homes, shops and restaurants. It refers to this commercial street, not the whole of Bophut Beach.

faq: Does Fisherman’s Village mean all of Bophut Beach?
No. It refers to the commercial street along Bophut Beach, lined with former fishing-village homes, shops and restaurants. It is a place for a street stroll rather than a beach-swimming visit.
What can I see there?

You will find shops, accommodation and restaurants in old wooden shophouses belonging to the Chinese community, along with souvenir shops selling hand-carved soap, wooden ornaments, ceramics and bags.
Can I have a meal there?
Restaurants along the coast road serve seafood and international dishes. After looking around the shops and old houses, you can have dinner at a restaurant near the water.
